summary: Defines DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), which lets a signing domain take responsibility for an email message using public-key cryptography and keys published in the DNS. Receivers can check the signature to verify the source and contents. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 6376.

plainLanguage.summary: A sender signs each letter with a special pen that only they have, and shows the receiver how to check the signature. If the letter was changed, the check fails.

questions: how to verify an email signature
subtitle: How a domain signs outgoing email and publishes the key in DNS so receivers can check the message.

tldr.problem: Email had no widely deployable way for a domain to take responsibility for a message, and existing signing schemes needed trusted certificate authorities or new infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: The signer hashes selected header fields and the body, signs the hash with an RSA private key, and adds a DKIM-Signature header field. The verifier fetches the public key from a DNS TXT record under _domainkey and checks the signature.
tldr.outcome: A failed or missing signature should not by itself cause rejection. This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 6376 and updated by RFC 5672.

today: RFC 4871 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6376, which is the DKIM signatures specification to use. It was also updated by RFC 5672.

sections.title: What DKIM Does and How It Differs
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) lets a signing domain claim responsibility for a message by cryptographically signing it. Recipients query the signer's domain for the public key and confirm that the message was attested to by a party holding the matching private key.

The RFC contrasts DKIM with S/MIME and OpenPGP. The signature lives in a header field, so people and existing mail software are not confused by it in the body. There is no dependency on well-known certificate authorities or on new protocols for key distribution or revocation. Verification failure does not force rejection, there is no encryption, and message archiving is not a design goal.

DKIM separates the signer's identity from the message's purported author. The identity is carried in the signature, and verifiers decide what to do with it. The scheme is meant to be deployed incrementally and to allow signing to be delegated to third parties.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature is written on the envelope instead of inside the letter, and you do not need an official stamp office to check it. Just ask the sender's own office.

sections.title: The DKIM-Signature Header Field
sections.content:
The signature is stored in a DKIM-Signature header field whose value is a list of tag=value pairs. Unrecognized tags MUST be ignored, and tags are case sensitive.

  • v= the version, which MUST be 1.
  • a= the algorithm, either rsa-sha1 or rsa-sha256.
  • b= the signature data, in base64.
  • bh= the hash of the canonicalized body, in base64.
  • c= the canonicalization for header and body, defaulting to simple/simple.
  • d= the signing domain, which is the domain queried for the public key.
  • h= the colon-separated list of signed header fields, which MUST NOT be empty.

When computing or verifying, the b= value of the signature being processed is treated as an empty string, and that header field is included last in the hash.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature note lists who signed, how they signed, which parts of the letter they covered, and the signature itself.

sections.title: Algorithms and Canonicalization
sections.content:
Two signing algorithms are defined, rsa-sha1 and rsa-sha256. Verifiers MUST implement both, and signers MUST implement and SHOULD sign using rsa-sha256. Signers MUST use RSA keys of at least 1024 bits for long-lived keys, and verifiers MUST be able to validate keys from 512 bits to 2048 bits.

Mail servers sometimes change messages in transit, so DKIM first canonicalizes the message. For headers and body separately there are two choices. The simple algorithm tolerates almost no change. The relaxed algorithm tolerates common changes such as whitespace replacement and header re-wrapping, for example by lowercasing header names and collapsing runs of whitespace to a single space.

A signer may also limit the signed body to an initial number of octets with the l= tag, which helps when mailing lists append trailers. The RFC later lists this among the potential attack surfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail carriers sometimes straighten the spacing in your letter. Relaxed mode ignores that kind of tidying, and simple mode makes the check fail if even one space moved.

sections.title: Selectors and Keys in DNS
sections.content:
A domain can publish several public keys by using selectors, which subdivide the key namespace. Selectors might name offices, dates or even individual users. They let a domain delegate signing to a partner and let it rotate keys: publish both the old and new keys during a transition period, sign with the new private key, then remove the old public key. Signers are ill-advised to reuse a selector with a new key.

Keys are looked up in DNS TXT records under a subdomain named _domainkey. With d=example.com and selector foo.bar, the query is for foo.bar._domainkey.example.com. Implementations MUST support this binding, and a selector MUST have a unique TXT record.

By default a key for a domain can sign for any of its subdomains. The s flag in the key record's t= tag restricts it to exactly the signing identity's domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office of a company can have its own signing pen, listed in a public phone book under a name like "london". When a pen is retired, they take it out of the book.

sections.title: Signer and Verifier Actions
sections.content:
A signer may be a user agent, submission agent, mail transfer agent or mailing list. The message must be signed before it leaves the signer's administrative domain. The signer chooses a private key and selector, normalizes the message, picks the header fields to sign, computes the body hash and signature, and inserts the DKIM-Signature header field.

A verifier extracts the signatures, validates each signature header field, fetches the public key from DNS and computes the verification. The RFC recommends verifying promptly, ideally at the border MTA, and discourages deferring it until the end user opens the message. Order of multiple signatures has no ultimate meaning.

Verifiers SHOULD NOT reject a message solely because it lacks a signature or the signature fails to verify, since that would cause interoperability problems. If a verifier does reject during the SMTP session it SHOULD use a 550/5.7.x reply code. Only temporary failures such as an unreachable key server should get a 4xx reply, for example 451/4.7.5, and cryptographic failures MUST NOT return 4xx.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender stamps the letter before it leaves the building. The receiver looks up the sender's public stamp-checker and tests the stamp, but does not throw away a letter just because the stamp is missing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that any mechanism meant to stem spam will be attacked intensively. It discusses body length limits (the l= tag), misappropriated private keys, denial-of-service against key servers, attacks against the DNS, replay attacks, limits on revoking keys, malformed key records and signatures, information leakage, remote timing attacks, reordered header fields, RSA attacks and inappropriate signing by parent domains.

Two examples: malware on a user's computer that steals a private key could send signed mail as that user, which is why the RFC suggests sending through an outgoing MTA that authenticates the submitter. In a replay attack a spammer gets a message signed by a legitimate MTA and resends the unchanged message, with its valid signature, to many recipients. The partial remedy is reputation services and detecting unusual volumes of identical signed mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys can steal a signing pen or copy a real signed letter and mail it again and again, so receivers also need to watch who is sending too much.
